A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, figures, Table 1, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer experiments on synthetic random-string membership testing, including confidence distributions and empirical KL measurements in Section 4.3 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v5 retains these original synthetic experiments and their results in Section 4.3, Figures 1–4, and Appendix E.

M1.justification: The membership-testing framework, hash-based two-sided filter construction in Appendix D.3, and experimental Transformer architecture and weighted cross-entropy objective are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate factual membership through the same synthetic universe of length-15 strings over 26 letters. No dataset, domain, task requirement, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Both compare learned distributions against the same theoretical optimal distributions and memory bounds. Neither adds or removes an evaluated competing algorithm; the new citations are contextual references.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 1 retain 15,145 facts, model sizes of 8,767/15,145/33,085 parameters, four loss weights, 30,000 training epochs, 200,000 evaluation negatives, and 50-bin KL estimation. No evaluation setting changes.

E4.justification: The same model-size and loss-weight sweeps, hallucination-tail analysis, and comparison of empirical versus optimal KL remain in Section 4.3 and Appendix E. No additional ablation or robustness analysis appears.

E5.justification: Appendix E specifies seed 42 for all experiments in both versions. Neither introduces repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain identical plotted results. Both versions report approximately 12% KL overhead over the theoretical bound, effective memory near two bits per parameter, and the same hallucination and reweighting trends.

T1.justification: The formal assumptions, main theorems, Appendix A budget decomposition, and proofs in Appendices B–D are retained. Changes such as correcting ln X to ln x in Appendix C.2 and repairing a missing parenthesis are notation or typography fixes without revised mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same sparse-limit rate-distortion characterization, optimal hallucination-channel claim, and two-sided-filter memory trade-off. Expanded motivation does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Section 1.1 newly connects the steep memory cost of eliminating residual errors to aggregate-loss training incentives. Appendix A.2 adds the qualification that memorization can be necessary for generalization and explains how regularization can also exclude valuable long-tail facts.

D1.justification: Appendix E and Table 1 preserve the same tokenization, architecture, optimizer, precision, learning schedule, sampling, and evaluation details. Both still state that implementation code will be released publicly; no new access information is supplied.

R1.justification: v5 adds memorization references by Arpit et al., Brown et al., Feldman, Feldman and Zhang, and Feldman et al. It positions the work as complementary to necessary-memorization arguments and expands Section 1.2's distinction from calibration-based hallucination accounts.

P1.justification: v5 refines wording and grammar in the introduction, Section 4, and Appendix A, adds explanatory paragraphs, and introduces acknowledgements. The overall organization and exposition of the core theory and experiments remain intact.

P2.justification: The four figures and Table 1 retain their designs, panels, axes, legends, and captions. Text reflow changes their surrounding placement: Figure 1 moves from following Theorem 4.1 to interrupting Theorem 4.3 in v5, a limited layout change.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v5 gives a more balanced account of memorization in Appendix A.2 and explains more explicitly why aggregate-loss training may tolerate hallucinations in Section 1.1. These additions and the expanded research positioning modestly improve the motivation without changing the theoretical or empirical evidence. The gains outweigh minor layout drawbacks, particularly Figure 1 interrupting Theorem 4.3.
